newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek shares to correct, valuations pricey-Salomon.
newsitem.headline: Greek shares to correct, valuations pricey-Salomon.

text.p: Greek equities are likely to continue their correction in the next few months as valuations have been pushed to unattractive levels, said Salomon Brothers in its July strategy report which called for a neutral stance.
"We are neutral on Greece and Hungary in the short term -- valuations are no longer attractive," said emerging markets strategist Danielle Downing in the July investment strategy report.

Despite the June correction after five months of strong performance, Greek market valuations are in the high range of emerging market stocks and this may push international investors to reduce exposure to Greece in the short term.
The Athens bourse's benchmark share index lost 8.5 percent in $ terms in June, driven by price declines in large-cap stocks. OTE telecom fell by 5.0 percent.
The banking sector, the market's locomotive, saw declines across the board -- Ergobank down 26.5 percent, Alpha Credit Bank down 15.2 percent and National Bank down 13 percent.
"The only robust company performance was by Titan Cement whose share price appreciated by 93.6 percent for the month in $ terms," Salomon said.

Nonetheless, Greek equities are still the third best-performing market in the region and fifth in a global context for the year with a total appreciation of 42.6 percent based on the Greek IFCI index in $ terms, it said.
"In the medium term, we are convinced that the Greek economy will see moderate recovery and the government remains firmly committed to ensure that Greece joins EMU by 2001," strategist Downing said.

In the year to date, European emerging markets have been characterised by a stellar performance, with four of the markets in the region -- Russia, Turkey, Greece and Hungary -- ranking in the top five in a global context.

"We expect capital flows to emerging markets to be strong in the next three years, having witnessed their recovery from the 1994 Mexican crisis," she said adding that emerging economies could attract capital flows of up to $300 billion per annum in 1997-2000 versus $175 billion in 1994-96.

One of the reasons for the expected increase in funds flow to emerging markets is the steady growth in per capita pension fund assets in developed economies. More and more of these assets are invested internationally.

"Capital flows to emerging markets are also affected by trends in mature markets, particularly the U.S.. With such high valuations in the U.S. market, we expect an increase in asset allocation to emerging markets globally which would benefit emerging Europe."
